props.title: The Devil's Own
props.initialSlug: An unlikely alliance. A deadly game.

sections.content: **The Devil's Own** (1997) represents a crucial entry in the complex web of IRA-themed Hollywood films, arriving at a pivotal moment just before the Good Friday Agreement. Brad Pitt's portrayal of Frankie McGuire/Rory Devaney showcases the moral ambiguity that defined 90s political thrillers, while Harrison Ford delivers a grounded performance as Tom O'Meara, the unwitting host to an IRA operative. The film follows similar thematic territory as **Patriot Games** (1992) and **In the Name of the Father** (1993), but takes a more nuanced approach to the Irish conflict, refusing to paint either side as purely heroic or villainous.

sections.content: Director Alan J. Pakula, known for paranoid political thrillers like **All the President's Men** (1976), brings his characteristic tension to the domestic sphere. The film's strength lies in its exploration of how political violence invades personal spaces, similar to themes in **The Crying Game** (1992) and **Cal** (1984). The relationship between Pitt and Ford's characters creates a microcosm of the larger conflict, with trust and betrayal playing out against the backdrop of seemingly peaceful suburban America.

While production was famously troubled, with reported conflicts between Pitt and Ford, the film succeeds in capturing the complexity of late 90s Irish-American relations. Like **Some Mother's Son** (1996), it examines how violence ripples through families and communities. The film's release coincided with real-world peace negotiations, lending it additional historical weight and context. SUBHEAD: Impact on Irish Conflict Cinema

sections.content: **The Devil's Own** marked a turning point in Hollywood's treatment of the Irish conflict, moving away from the more straightforward action dynamics of films like **Blown Away** (1994) toward more morally complex territory. This shift would influence later works like **Fifty Dead Men Walking** (2008) and **'71** (2014), which continued to explore the human cost of political violence while avoiding simple good-versus-evil narratives.
